title: Netwealth turns to governance overhaul after First Guardian case
full_text:
On 17 December, ASIC commenced proceedings in the Federal Court against Netwealth Superannuation Services Pty Ltd (NSS) and Netwealth Investments Limited (NIL), as trustees of the Netwealth Superannuation Master Fund (NSMF).
Shortly after, Netwealth admitted it had failed in its responsibilities and agreed to pay $101 million in compensation to cover members who lost funds as a result of First Guardian being on the Netwealth platform.
ASIC said at the time: “NSS and NIL have admitted they failed to obtain and therefore did not assess sufficient information about the First Guardian Master Fund, or make sufficient independent enquiries, to understand or evaluate the investment risk in the First Guardian Diversified Class and Growth Class prior to or while offering them as investment options to NSMF members.”
The case concluded on 20 August with Justice McEvoy of the Federal Court issuing judgement that Netwealth had “failed to do all things necessary to ensure that the financial services covered by its financial services licence were provided efficiently, honestly and fairly”.
Netwealth had, the court papers seen by ifa stated, contravened sections 912A(1)(a) and 912A(5A) of the Corporations Act 2001.
The Court found that NIL “did not obtain and, therefore, did not assess sufficient information about the FGMF, and did not make sufficient independent enquiries, to understand or evaluate investment risk in the First Guardian Diversified Strategies Class (Diversified Class) or the First Guardian Growth Strategies Class (Growth Class) investment options prior to or while offering those investment options to members with an interest in the NSMF’s Super Accelerator Plus product”.
In these circumstances, it stated that NIL had approved the Diversified Class and Growth Class investment options to be made available to members for selection and that, while NSMF trustee, had made investments in these products at the direction of members up to an investment limit of 100 per cent of the member’s account.
According to the Judge, NSMF trustee also failed to inform its members of the potential illiquidity of the Diversified Class and Growth Class investment options while they were offered to members.
As a result, Netwealth has been ordered to pay the plaintiff’s – ASIC’s – costs of the proceeding as agreed, or in the absence of agreement, to be taxed.
This is in addition to the $101 million paid in compensation to members, as agreed, on 30 January.
ASIC chair Sarah Court said: “Superannuation trustees are a critical safeguard for Australians’ retirement savings and must undertake rigorous due diligence before making investment options available to members.
“In this case, Netwealth admitted it failed to obtain sufficient information about First Guardian and failed to undertake sufficient enquiries to properly understand the risks associated with First Guardian.
“Following ASIC’s investigation, Netwealth compensated affected members, providing certainty to more than 1,000 Australians whose retirement savings were exposed to significant harm. Today’s outcome sends a clear message that superannuation trustees must put members first and take proactive steps to identify and respond to investment risks before members suffer harm.”
Netwealth chief executive Matt Heine said in an ASX statement: “The agreed outcome, now confirmed by the court, allows us to move forward and continue our work in supporting out members, our clients and our business.
“The compensation payments provided by Netwealth means affected members’ superannuation accounts had the net capital invested in First Guardian returned, alleviating distress caused by the collapse.”
Part of Netwealth’s response to the fallout has also seen NSS agree to an enforceable undertaking with the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) requiring an uplift of its investment governance processes which are to be overseen by an independent expert.
Subsequently, the firm said Program RISE – Reviewing Investment Standards and Excellence – was established by NSS to “review and further uplift onboarding and monitoring processes in relation to the investment options we make available to our members”.
Heine added: “NSS is delivering on the key milestones agreed under the APRA enforceable undertaking. We are increasing our investment and prioritising continuous improvement of the investment governance framework for the benefit of superannuation members including greater integration of investment governance and adviser oversight activities and improved transparency of the review and monitoring of investment options.
“We believe these initiatives, along with our engagement with the industry via the Financial Services Council to support fit for purpose regulations and standards, will result in improved protections of members’ interests in the future.”
